title: Your AI Configurator Is Only as Good as Your Rules
text: Medium Your AI Configurator Is Only as Good as Your Rules | by Kalyani Wasave | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in A new waiter, the same kitchen Five places configuration data breaks What I’d fix before turning AI on Five numbers to check first The people behind the rules Sources Kalyani Wasave Manufacturing Supply Chain Artificial Intelligence Product Management Data Governance Your AI Configurator Is Only as Good as Your Rules Kalyani Wasave 5 min read · Oct 9, 2026 -- Listen Share Why the rules and product data underneath decide whether AI quoting works. Press enter or click to view image in full size Every CPQ vendor I follow is talking about AI agents this year. The pitch is easy to like. A buyer types what they need in plain words, and the agent turns it into a complete, priced product in seconds. No sales rep, no waiting for a quote. I’ve worked with product configuration data in manufacturing, so my first question wasn’t how fast it is. It was: which rules is it reading? An AI configurator doesn’t invent your product. It works from the rules and data you already have. If those are solid, the agent looks brilliant. If they’re messy, it repeats the mess, only faster and to more customers. A new waiter, the same kitchen The easiest way I’ve found to explain this is a restaurant. The AI agent is a new waiter. He speaks every language, never mishears an order and can serve a hundred tables at once. But he reads from the same menu as everyone else. If the menu still lists the salmon and the kitchen ran out yesterday, he’ll promise salmon to every table. Politely, and very fast. Press enter or click to view image in full size That’s roughly what’s being sold right now. Threekit describes agents that take a buyer “from product discovery through a fully validated, rules-compliant configuration” without a rep. Epicor, Infor, Tacton and Salesforce are adding similar features. One example Threekit gives is a buyer typing “I need something that handles 200 PSI in a wet environment,” and the agent working out which options fit. What surprised me is how openly the vendors admit the catch. In Threekit’s own words: “AI configurators are only as good as the product data and constraint logic that feed them.” Tacton makes a similar point. Configurators have run on rule-based logic for decades, and the agent is a new front end on top of those rules. It doesn’t replace them. Five places configuration data breaks This isn’t a niche worry. In a January 2025 survey of 656 manufacturing executives by Aras , product complexity (46%), tracking changes over time (36%) and extensive configurations (35%) were the top problems with connected product data. Aras sells PLM software, so I’d read that with some care, but the pattern is familiar. Press enter or click to view image in full size Here’s where I’d expect things to go wrong first. 1. A rule nobody wrote down. Most catalogs have a rule like “never pair this option with that one.” It sits in a spreadsheet, an old email or someone’s memory. A person at the order desk catches it every time. An AI agent never will, because it was never in the system. 2. Sellable, but not buildable. A component gets retired, but nobody switches off the option that uses it. The configurator keeps offering a product the factory can’t make anymore. 3. A change that stopped halfway. An engineering change swaps a part in the BOM. The price and the rule that depend on it stay the same. Now the quote and the build don’t match. 4. No lead time on the option. Lots of options carry a price but no time. A made-to-order build gets the same delivery date as a standard one, and the agent promises a date the plant can’t hit. 5. One option, three names. It’s a short code on the dealer portal, a word in the configurator and a part number in the ERP. People translate between them without thinking. An agent working across all three has to guess. None of these are new problems. What changes is the speed. Someone entering ten orders a day catches a few of them out of habit. An agent quoting a thousand a day catches none. What I’d fix before turning AI on You don’t need a perfect catalog. You need one where the rules in the system match the rules in people’s heads. If I were starting tomorrow, this is roughly the order I’d go in: Sit down with sales, engineering and the order desk, and write down every “we never do that.” Then get each one into the configurator. Keep a small set of test orders, maybe 20 to 50, that you know should pass or fail. Run them every time a rule changes. Software teams do this with code all the time, and it works just as well for configurations. Don’t close an engineering change until someone has checked the options, prices and rules it affects. Look at low-volume and unused options every quarter, and retire the ones you don’t build anymore. Agree on one name for each option, and map every channel to it. Give every option a lead time, not just a price. Put a name next to every rule. If nobody owns a rule, nobody updates it. It isn’t exciting work. But it decides whether the AI looks smart or embarrassing in front of a customer. Five numbers to check first Before anyone signs an AI contract, I’d want a baseline for these five. Press enter or click to view image in full size Here’s how I’d work each one out: Configuration accuracy. Configured orders that needed no fix to the BOM, price or lead time, divided by all configured orders. Rule test pass rate. Test orders that gave the expected result, divided by all test orders. Dead options. Active options with no orders in 12 months, or that use a retired part. Change-to-rule lag. Days between an engineering change and the matching configurator update. Rules outside the system. Rules you find in spreadsheets, emails or people’s heads. If these aren’t getting better month to month, putting AI on top just makes the gaps easier to see. And it’ll be your customers
